```sql
-- PostgreSQL; assumes the table is named users.
BEGIN;

ALTER TABLE users
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS first_name text,
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS last_name  text;

-- Only touches rows not yet backfilled, so a second run changes nothing
-- and never overwrites names edited after the first run.
UPDATE users
SET first_name = substring(btrim(full_name) from '^\S+'),
    last_name  = substring(btrim(full_name) from '^\S+\s+(.*)$')
WHERE full_name IS NOT NULL
  AND first_name IS NULL
  AND last_name IS NULL;

COMMIT;
```

This has not been run against a database.

It splits on the first whitespace, so "Mary Ann Smith" becomes `Mary` / `Ann Smith`, and a single-word name leaves `last_name` NULL.

I left `full_name` in place; drop it in a later migration once nothing reads it.

The backfill is one `UPDATE` in one transaction, which is fine for small tables; on a table with millions of rows, batch it by primary key range to avoid a long row lock.
